en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by imperial decree: Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, and also with an assembly of five thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. These bodhisattvas had attained great forbearance and unimpeded eloquence; they had subdued Māra and his enmity and constrained all non-Buddhists; they had resolved their minds upon the Great Way, attained samādhi, and possessed mastery over dhāraṇīs; they were endowed with the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and had thoroughly realized the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) as well as the most supreme and profound *pāramitās*. They had even penetrated all Buddha-dharmas and immeasurable, boundless virtues and merits. Their names were as follows:

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Samantanetra Bodhisattva, Samantadarśin Bodhisattva, Samantaprabha Bodhisattva, Samantāvabhāsa Bodhisattva, Adhyāśaya Bodhisattva, Vardhamānāśaya Bodhisattva, Anantāśaya Bodhisattva, Vipulāśaya Bodhisattva, Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, Dharaṇīdhara Bodhisattva, Lokottara Bodhisattva, Jitāśaya Bodhisattva, Anuttarāśaya Bodhisattva, Dhāraṇīśvararāja Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, and others—furthermore, accompanied by sixteen persons including Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and his peers;

Furthermore, there were Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World; Śakra, the Lord of Devas; and the Four Great Kings who protect the world. Also present were the Devaputra Suśimi and the Devaputra Aniya, along with various kings of devas, nāgas, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, yakṣas, and garuḍas, each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues, all coming together to sit in the assembly.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the Lion Throne of the Auspicious Treasury, surrounded by the fourfold assembly in numbers exceeding Mount Sumeru. His radiance was blazing and intense, illuminating the entire world like the sun and the moon;
his deportment was perfect and his holy life was tranquil, like Śakra among the devas whose deportment is most supreme;
and he was like a wheel-turning monarch endowed with the seven treasures, free from all fears like a lion king.

He is skillfully able to discourse upon the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena, like a great mass of fire that destroys all darkness, or like the king of mani-jewels that shines far upon everything.
In this way, the Buddha’s light illuminates all worlds within the trichiliocosm; from within that light, he issues a wondrous Brahma-voice to address all sentient beings:

"The supreme *pāramitā* of all dharmas which I have now attained—I shall proclaim its true meaning. It is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its words and meaning are sublime, pure and perfect, a holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is stainless and unadulterated."

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Joy sat serenely amidst the great assembly. Beholding the World-Honored One upon the lion throne emitting a great radiance—like the thousand suns illuminating all things—he was filled with great joy, deep faith, and reverence. Rising from his seat, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and praised him in verse:
“The Buddha’s body shines brilliantly like a mountain of gold; His benefit to the world is most rare and marvelous.
The Sangha of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, Along with devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, all surround him.”
Just as Mount Sumeru is the abode of the gods, rising high and manifest above the great ocean,
so do you manifest your body out of compassion for sentient beings, emitting hundreds of thousands of rays of light that shine eternally.
Practicing the conduct of Brahmā, he is indeed Brahmā; among those Brahmās, he is further their king.
Practicing dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi, his light illuminates the bodhisattvas of the higher stages.
Just as Śakra is the Lord of Devas, distinguished by his majesty, deportment, and various marks,
so too does the Muni’s radiance illuminate the world, distinguished by his physical excellences and meritorious virtues.

The Golden Wheel-turning King attains sovereignty over the four continents, Skillfully taming all sentient beings and leading those multitudes out of the wheel of suffering; The compassion of our Buddha is likewise so.
All the light of fire, the light of mani-jewels, The light of the sun and moon, and all such radiances—
Even the light of hundreds of thousands of suns Cannot equal the constant illumination of the Buddha-sun.
Just as the moon in the night releases its radiance, universally illuminating the world until all is pure;
so too the Buddha’s face is as majestic and serene as the full moon, outshining all other lights so they no longer appear.
Just as a great fire burning upon a high mountain can shatter the darkness of night and reveal all directions,
so too does the light of wisdom possessed by the Great Sage utterly destroy the darkness and transcend all realms of existence.
Just as when the great lion roars in the wilderness, all the beasts are struck with terror upon hearing it;
so too are all the māras when they hear the Buddha preach the meaning of the emptiness of phenomena and non-self.
The Mani-jewel king emits radiance, Causing all other mani-jewels to lose their luster;
The Buddha’s body shines with true golden color, Outshining all the lights of the world.
Among all those who are wise and noble in the world, there is none superior to the Buddha;
endowed with merit, diligence, skillful means, and wisdom, his every virtue is immeasurable.

Beholding the Great Master’s ocean of merit, whose majestic radiance shines universally upon all sentient beings, I single-mindedly revere and long for his honored countenance; therefore, I now prostrate with my head at his feet.
The mind of praise, admiration, and reverence for the Buddha— whose worldly merits are peerless—
I dedicate it all within the Dharma-realm, so that all in every world may attain the path of Buddhahood.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Joy, having praised the Buddha, joined his palms toward the Buddha and gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, his eyes never for a moment turning away.

One contemplates the dharma-realm with the mind—its meaning is profoundly deep, difficult to know and difficult to see, transcending words and conceptualization, cutting off all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*), subtle and hard to understand, and inconceivable. Thus one contemplates and visualizes the entire dharma-realm as being apprehended and directly realized through the wisdom of vision of only the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; the realm of the Buddha is peerless. Thus one perceives that all the inconceivable realms of skillful means of the Tathāgatas are subsumed within the single characteristic of the nature of the dharma-realm.
Just as space has no place of abiding, so too is the realm of sentient beings like its own nature;
all phenomena are likewise thus: unimpeded liberation, ultimate quiescence.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, through their skillful means, transform their bodies so that Buddha-fields fill all places and manifest before the eyes of sentient beings; yet the bodies of these Tathāgatas cannot be apprehended even throughout incalculable koṭis of kalpas.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Joy had thus contemplated the merits of the Buddha, he remained silent.
Then there was a venerable one named Guardian of the Nation (Rāṣṭrapāla) who was observing the three-month rains retreat in the great city of Śrāvastī.

When this summer retreat had passed, he donned his robes, took up his bowl, and together with the bhikṣus, those who had newly gone forth, and those who had first resolved their minds, departed from Śrāvastī and proceeded to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha.

Having reached that mountain, the Venerable Guardian of the Nation (Rāṣṭrapāla) immediately proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side. With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these verses in praise of the Buddha:
"Homage to the supreme light of the Buddha; Homage to the unimpeded mind like space;
Homage to the one who can sever all fetters and bonds; Homage to the one who has forever transcended the ocean of the three realms of existence."
The Buddha’s boundless and true form and marks pervade billions of lands;
having heard this, the Bodhisattvas come with joy to reverently make offerings to the Buddha’s merit.
Having performed this supreme offering, they listened to the Muni’s Dharma, free from all defilements;
each giving rise to joy, they returned to their own lands, praising the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One.
Having traversed countless koṭis of eons, Bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings,
Their body and mind never grow weary, In pursuit of unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment.
Constantly practicing generosity, the observance of precepts, patience, diligence, the gateway of meditative concentration,
and wisdom with skillful means to reach nirvāṇa— for this reason, I pay homage to the Great Awakened Honored One.
Having accomplished the six supernormal powers, the four bases of psychic power, the faculties, the ten powers, and the gates of liberation—
through these practices and for the sake of all sentient beings, I now pay homage to the Buddha’s peerless wisdom.
The Unsurpassed World-Honored One fully perceives and beholds the minds of all beings in the world, their conduct, their deeds,
and the karma they accomplish, as well as all their physical actions, speech, and expressions.
Unable to sever the faults of greed and delusion, sentient beings fall into the three realms of existence because of them;
yet through the Buddha, they accomplish the karma of the Sugata, being able to discern all that is wholesome and unwholesome in the world.
All the deeds of the Buddhas of the past, And those of the Teachers of Gods and Humans in the present,
Even unto the oceans of merit in the future— He fully knows all these phenomena;
Surrounded by pure lands and multitudes, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
Even the lifespans of all Buddhas, my Buddha can know them all;
All phenomena of arising and ceasing, All offerings made as Buddha-works,
And all dharmas of the Dharma-treasury that are upheld— My Buddha can know them all.
The Buddha possesses the ten powers and unimpeded wisdom, Ever abiding in the present throughout the three periods of time;
To all such methods of skillful means, I pay homage to the World-Honored One, the ocean of wisdom.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One is peerless, Adorned with the marks and signs of great auspiciousness.
Like the multitude of stars appearing in the sky at night, I pay homage to the Muni, the Most Honored One.
His physical marks are so majestic and sublime that none can equal them;
his radiance illuminates all the heavens and the world, such that Śakra, Brahmā, and the gods of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven do not appear before him when they stand in the presence of the Buddha.
Stainless and immovable like a mountain of gold, with right-turning, coiled topknots deep blue and lustrous;
the Buddha’s crown is lofty and prominent like a mountain of gold, its radiance shining afar to produce all blessings;
light pervades billions of nayutas, manifesting the white tuft-mark between the eyebrows.
Your eyes are like blue lotuses, ever serene and joyful; You observe the world with a mind imbued with compassion.
Like the pure full moon in the midst of space, The Buddha’s face is likewise perfectly radiant.
All who behold it can never tire of the sight; I pay homage to the Tathāgata’s perfect features.
Your gait is like that of the king of geese or the king of deer; Like the king of oxen, your stride is steady and firm.
You shake the great earth without ceasing for a moment; I pay homage to the Tathāgata’s steadfast power.
Your fingers are slender and long, marked by webbed lines; Your nails are pure and bright, like refined red copper.
Standing upright with hands hanging down reaching past his knees, I pay homage to the Golden-Colored Great Awakened Honored One.
As the Buddha walks upon the great earth, auspicious signs appear; he is fully endowed with the manifestation of the thousand-spoked wheel.
His feet emit radiance that illuminates all living beings; those who receive this light are all able to be reborn in the celestial realms.
The Great Sage, the Dharma King, bestows the seven riches; As a donor, he is able to maintain a mind of equanimity.
Taming and guiding the world, he acts in accordance with the Dharma; I pay homage to the Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Awakened One.
With compassion and the Dharma-mind as sword, And the bow of ethical discipline, skillful means, and wisdom,
One can sever the various bandits of affliction, So that birth, death, and saṃsāra no longer increase.
Having fulfilled the fruit of self-benefit, one further benefits others, Causing those sentient beings likewise to attain liberation;
Ultimately bringing peace and joy, emerging from the dust and toil of saṃsāra, They shall enter the tranquil teaching of the Sugata.
Without birth, without cessation, and without all sufferings, Nor with birth, old age, or separation from loved ones—
Such is the Unconditioned, the Supreme Vehicle, Which the Buddha has preached out of compassion for sentient beings.
I praise the Supreme Great Sage, who encompasses all the qualities of the Buddhas;
by all such merits as these, may all sentient beings realize Bodhi.

At that time, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, having praised the Buddha with verses, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and paid respectful homage; he then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!”
"I have a question; I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant me leave to ask it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"Regarding what you have asked, I shall explain it for you, fulfilling your request and causing you to give rise to joy."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the Venerable Rakṣita felt joy in both body and mind and spoke these words:
“World-Honored One!

What dharmas constitute the complete practice of a bodhisattva, by which one may attain all supreme merits, unimpeded great wisdom, and definitive eloquence; clearly understand natures and characteristics, enter into all-knowledge to transform sentient beings, sever their ignorance, delusive thoughts, and afflictions, and become certain of the truth; enter into all-knowledge, utter true speech, and cause those sentient beings to act according to what they have heard, leave behind all darkness and folly, and through the skillful means of recollecting the Buddha, delight in hearing all profound Brahma-meanings, uphold all dharmas, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?”
At that time, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“The conduct practiced by Bodhisattvas is a definitive practice; That practice must necessarily possess the true Dharma.
This true Dharma arises from the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom; May the Supreme Tathāgata explain it to me.”
The Buddha’s body radiates the luster of golden light, A supreme and boundless mass of great merit;
To deliver all sentient beings of the six realms, He proclaims the stainless conduct of the bodhisattvas.
How can one attain the inexhaustible wisdom of great enlightenment, The dhāraṇī that gives birth to the nectar of bodhi?
How can one attain the ocean of pure wisdom?
That wisdom is able to sever the doubts of sentient beings.
For many koṭis of kalpas, sentient beings have wandered in the suffering of saṃsāra, their minds wearyless in their delusion and drowning;
beholding them thus deluded and assailed by affliction, how can one cultivate the ten wholesome paths for their sake?
The buddha-field is pure and the assembly is full; the true field is boundless and his lifespan is long.
For the sake of the multitude, he constantly proclaims subtle and wondrous words; may you now speak of the stainless practice of bodhi.
Subduing malevolent spirits and giving rise to right view, Drying up that river of craving to realize liberation,
The pure Dharma-eye illuminates the ignorant and blind, Causing all sentient beings to practice the supreme path.
Majestic, noble, and possessed of great eloquence, your speech is gentle and brings joy to all who hear it;
like nectar that moistens the world, may you preach the profound and subtle Dharma.
Your Brahma-voice is deep and wondrous, severing all evils, and its tone is harmonious and elegant like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
The assembly seeking the Dharma has gathered at the Buddha’s place; I pray you will preach the nectar to deliver all living beings.
Among the multitude are those with the supreme faculties for Bodhi, as well as those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha natures;
I pray that the Buddha will teach according to their faculties through skillful means, for the meeting of teacher and disciple is indeed the right time.
I now delight in hearing the Supreme Vehicle; only the Buddha knows my bodhi-nature.
I take no pleasure in seeking this Lesser Vehicle; I pray that you will expound the Tathāgata’s foremost Dharma.
At that time, after the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla had spoken these verses, the Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!

Venerable one, you have been able to question the Tathāgata regarding the most supreme meaning, benefiting many people so that they may attain peace and happiness, and sustaining all future bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
"Listen now attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you.
Then the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla said, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to hear this; I only pray that you will explain it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"There are four kinds of dharmas; when these are fully perfected in purity, one is called a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
“What are the four dharmas?
First, the internal; second, the external; third, the mind; and fourth, the intellect.

These four dharmas accord with principle and reality; seeing all sentient beings with a mind of equality—like space, free from discrimination—and acting in accordance with these words, this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s attainment of purity through the four kinds of dharmas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Mind, thought, internal, and external are ever pure; The mind of the true path to Bodhi never regresses.
Whatever good one performs is not in vain, And one shall attain the boundless wisdom of a Bodhisattva.”
Observing that those sentient beings suffer and lack a self, Being assailed on all sides by birth, old age, sickness, and death— Thus,
within this great ocean of the three realms of existence, You extensively ply the Dharma-ship to rescue all classes of beings.
Beholding all sentient beings with an impartial mind, I view this world as if it were my only child;
May I cause them all to attain liberation together, And turn them all toward bodhicitta without ever regressing.
Constantly expounding the meaning of emptiness and practicing in reliance upon emptiness, there is neither person nor self, nor sentient beings;
like dreams, illusions, and the like, they are without reality, thereby causing those who are deluded and ignorant to give rise to wisdom.
As the wisdom of the Great Awakened One has been proclaimed, one should act according to that wisdom;
subduing faults and bringing the mind to tranquility, one seeks to realize enlightenment as a child of the Buddha.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that bring peace and reassurance to the minds of bodhisattvas."
What are these four dharmas?
First, to aspire to seek and study the dharma-gate of dhāraṇī;
second, to constantly associate with virtuous friends and maintain flawless deportment.
Third, seeking to realize the profound patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
fourth, diligently practicing the pure observance of the precepts.
These four dharmas cause that bodhisattva to find solace in their mind, advancing in practice without regression.
He further spoke in verse:
"If a person loves and honors the dharma of dhāraṇī, Their fame will resound afar and they will be sought by all;
They can uphold this unsurpassed, wondrous gateway to the Dharma, As taught in common by all Tathāgatas."
Wisdom increases and becomes luminous, free from forgetfulness;
thus one swiftly attains unimpeded knowledge, penetrating all supreme dharmas, and accomplishes the gate of unconditioned liberation.

All attain enlightenment through virtuous friends; they give rise to the seven factors of awakening to cultivate abandonment, increase the eightfold noble path to perform the work of a Buddha, and distance themselves from evil friends as they would fear fire.
Hearing the profound Dharma, they realize non-arising;
They are able to understand that all phenomena are ultimately empty— Without self, without person, and without sentient beings— Thus forever departing from all views.
The Vinaya gives birth to all roots of goodness; by firmly upholding and guarding it, one remains free from transgression.
Such practice can bring about a mind of tranquility, as the Buddha personally proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that cause the minds of bodhisattvas to find delight while within saṃsāra."
What are these four dharmas?

First, causing all bodhisattvas to delight in seeing the Buddha; second, causing all bodhisattvas to delight in the preaching of the Dharma; third, causing all bodhisattvas to delight in being able to relinquish all that they possess; and fourth, causing all bodhisattvas to delight in the seal of patience regarding the profound dharma of signlessness.
"These four dharmas cause bodhisattvas to develop a deep sense of joy and attachment toward saṃsāra.
He further spoke in verse:
"When bodhisattvas behold the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, They practice the correct conduct throughout all their births."
Able to skillfully subdue all worlds, His radiance shines everywhere, dispelling the darkness of ignorance.
Thus making offerings to the Honored One among Men, With deep affection and joy, one always respects him;
He rescues and delivers all sentient beings, Causing them to enter the unsurpassed path of Bodhi.
If one hears the Dharma taught by all Buddhas, Body and mind become tranquil and give rise to joyful love;
With such a firm mind free from retreat, One will practice accordingly and swiftly realize the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Able to relinquish everything with a heart free from stinginess, Seeing those who come to beg, they give rise to joy;
Giving away their kingdoms, cities, wives, children, and even their own lives, They bestow these upon sentient beings as the cause for Buddhahood.
If one hears the profound Dharma of signlessness, Whose nature is free from discrimination and primordially empty—
Devoid of self, devoid of person, devoid of sentient beings— One will thus give rise to love and joy for it.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of things that bodhisattvas should not take pleasure in."
What are these four dharmas?

First, one should not take delight in the life of a householder; second, having already left the home-life, one should not take delight in gain and offerings; third, one should not take delight in being born into a noble clan; fourth, one should not take delight in those of the Lesser Vehicle.
"These four things, O Bodhisattvas, should not be cherished.
He further spoke in verse:
"The household life has boundless great faults; Abandon it so that the mind has nothing to which it clings."
Always delighting in the seclusion of mountains and wilds, with senses stilled, Bravely and diligently cultivating great wisdom and virtue,
Walking alone in purity like a sharp sword, Able to sever all stains of ignorance and delusion.
Regarding those various great gains and offerings, he always delights in remaining detached and free from attachment;
having renounced noble and eminent lineages, he views them as being like illusions, mirages, and the like.
Universally for the sake of all sentient beings, they practice giving, ethical discipline, patience, and all other such deeds;
not sparing even their own bodies, lives, or retinues, they aspire to seek perfect enlightenment and reach the further shore.
Having no attachment to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, they remain ever firm in the Supreme Vehicle;
even if their bodies were to be cut to pieces, their minds would not be broken, remaining as indestructible as a diamond.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that cause the decline of bodhisattvas."
What are these four dharmas?
First, violating and breaking the precepts;
second, not dwelling in mountain retreats while seeking tranquility.
Third, not relying on the teachings of the four vehicles but seeking them through false and deluded means;
fourth, although delighting in much learning, attaining nothing at all.
These four factors cause the decline of bodhisattvas.
He further spoke in verse:
"The characteristics of the precepts are as pure as a mani gem; They can lead sentient beings to the other shore.
If a bodhisattva here violates the code of discipline, They will remain lost and fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment."
Dwelling in a mountain hermitage of tranquil seclusion, the discriminations of self and person naturally vanish;
regarding men, women, retinues, and one’s own body as being like grass and trees, one is free from affectionate attachment.
The teachings and principles of the four vehicles are without falsehood; With a single mind of purity, practice according to the instructions.
One will surely attain the fullness of all merits And become a Great Being endowed with Buddha-wisdom.
Beholding those sentient beings in saṃsāra, Constantly dwelling in birth, death, grief, lamentation, and suffering,
I shall perpetually ply the supreme and wondrous Dharma-boat To ferry those sentient beings across the ocean of misery.
If those sentient beings were not rescued, they would remain lost and submerged in saṃsāra without end;
therefore, the Hīnayāna is not the ultimate goal, and for the sake of living beings, one must cause them to resolve upon bodhicitta.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that bodhisattvas should clearly understand and cultivate."
What are these four dharmas?
First, to give rise to the mind of equality of all Buddhas and seek the Sugata;
second, to serve the Dharma-preacher with respect and offerings, without attachment to bedding and other requisites.
Third, not coveting gain or offerings, nor having any further desires;
fourth, being fully accomplished in the patient endurance of the profound Dharma.
These four dharmas should be clearly understood and cultivated.
He further spoke in verse:
"There is a Sugata, a Great Being, Whom none can equal among gods or men;
He impartially guides all living beings, Thus practicing and cultivating the ten wholesome paths."
Respectfully serving the Dharma Master, practicing according to the teacher’s instructions,
and making great offerings to seek the Buddha-wisdom— through this, one also gives birth to the boundless Buddhas.
Dwelling eternally in deep mountains without fear, He gives rise to no greed for gain or honor therein;
Skillfully accomplishing unimpeded wisdom, He penetrates the profound Dharma and leaves all defilements behind.
Hearing of the Buddha’s merits, they rejoice deeply;
practicing the Dharma in this way with steadfastness, they realize that śānti of non-arising and extensively deliver sentient beings from immeasurable suffering.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that purify the practices of all bodhisattvas."
What are these four dharmas?
First, with body and mind resolute, seeking enlightenment with determination, one practices the purity of the Dharma;
second, free from all delusions, delighting in dwelling in deep mountains, one practices the purity of the Dharma.
Third, they are able to relinquish everything without seeking karmic retribution, thus practicing the purity of the Dharma;
fourth, they constantly follow Dharma masters day and night to seek the Dharma, thus practicing the purity of the Dharma.
"These four dharmas constitute the purification of the practices of all bodhisattvas.
He then spoke in verse:
"The stains of greed, hatred, and delusion are all exhausted in the mind; Laziness and falsehood are likewise absent."
Causing all faults to never arise again, he resolutely seeks to realize the path to Bodhi.
Disenchanted with his original home, the root of his sorrow severed, he abandons those worldly dusts and seeks to leave the household life.
Meeting no evil companions, he dwells and travels in deep mountains, tending toward liberation.
Cultivating pure conduct within those mountains, they are able to accomplish the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom;
with no attachment to body, life, or wealth, they are sovereign and fearless like lions.
Seeing those sentient beings, he gives rise to joy, Like birds gathering and then dispersing;
Observing that this world is not a place for long dwelling, He thus seeks the path to great bodhi.
Body and mind are pure like space; in relinquishing all things, there is no fear or alarm.
One has no attachment to gain or honor, just as a startled deer does not linger upon the ground.
The world constantly dwells in great peril and hardship; it is difficult to arouse body and mind to seek liberation.
Seeing that this is illusory and devoid of reality, I therefore practice the path of tranquility.
Always using gentle speech to entice all beings, regarding enemies and kin with equal impartiality and without discrimination,
free from attachment and dwelling nowhere like the wind— this is the supreme practice sought by Bodhisattvas.
Through the signless liberation, emptiness, and wishlessness, one realizes that all conditioned phenomena are like illusions and transformations;
constantly practicing with a pure and vast mind, one drinks the nectar of immortality and is ever joyful.
One who aspires to seek the Dharma by relying on a teacher, That person’s five aggregates are ever pure;
Though oppressed by manifold sufferings, they feel no fatigue, Thus attaining entry into the gateway of dhāraṇī.
Understanding this practice of the bodhisattva path, one accomplishes what is sought to bring joy to others;
yet if a person does not seek awakening, they possess little wisdom and shall lose it for a hundred lifetimes.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that constitute difficult dharmas for bodhisattvas."
What are these four dharmas?
First, the mind lacks respect and frequently acts with contempt;
second, the mind lacks filial conduct, being indolent and rebellious.
Third, the mind covets gain and offerings, lacking contentment;
fourth, the mind delights in falsehood, seeking wealth and profit through improper means.
These four dharmas constitute difficulties for a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"The Buddha, the Dharma, the Original Teacher, and one's parents— Lacking all faith and respect, they are mostly full of contempt;
Failing to practice filial piety, their minds are indolent, And they constantly act with folly and distraction."
Constantly coveting gain and offerings;
further practicing falsehood for the sake of perverse profit;
praising one's own virtues and deeds while slandering others:
"I can maintain the precepts and practice cultivation.
Yet they engage in mutual strife without compassion, Concealing their own faults while seeing the errors of others;
Furthermore, they pursue agriculture and business— Such śramaṇas possess no merit.
In the age of the final dharma, people will be distracted, Engaging in strife, killing one another, and harboring jealousy;
Śramaṇas will cause the Tathāgata’s Dharma to vanish, And all virtuous bhikṣus will distance themselves from it.
The wondrous path to bodhi will never again be encountered, And the cycle of the five destinies will have no end.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
“Furthermore, there are four kinds of things that bodhisattvas should avoid.”
What are these four dharmas?
First, indolence; second, lack of faith; third, envy; and fourth, harboring hatred toward others.
"These four dharmas should be avoided.
He further spoke in verse:
"Without faith, lazy, and deluded in mind; Harboring jealousy and constantly full of anger."
Seeing a śramaṇa who maintains patience, they drive him back and expel him from the monastery.
Toward people in this world, whether noble or base, they make no distinction between good and evil;
they act solely on the basis of right and wrong. Such faults arise from anger.
Far removed from the Buddha-dharma and its manifold virtues, They fall into the great fiery pits of the evil realms.
Such is the conduct that leads to the lower destinies; Failing to rely on the teachings, they incur this suffering.
Therefore, always practice the path to enlightenment, So as not to sink into rebirth within the evil realms.
The Great Sage who benefits sentient beings appears in the world only once every many koṭis of eons;
now that you have briefly encountered the Muni, quickly abandon all faults and seek liberation.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that a bodhisattva should not practice."
What are these four dharmas?

First, one should not associate with persons who are evil friends; second, one should not associate with persons who hold [wrong] views; third, one should not associate with persons who have abandoned all wholesome dharmas; fourth, one should not associate with persons who are attached to wealth and profit.
"One should not associate with these four kinds of persons.
He further spoke in verse:
"If a person stays far away from all evil friends, They will always find good friends coming to draw near."
Like the full moon appearing in the sky at night, it dispels darkness and reveals the path to Bodhi.
Whatever is seen is never interrupted; by nurturing one's own body and life, such poisonous vapors can be kept far away, and that person shall attain the great wisdom of Buddhahood.
If one abandons the most supreme and subtle Dharma, And takes no delight in the nectar-like flavor of tranquility,
Such a person is called an impure vessel, Far removed from seeking the realization of great Bodhi.
Craving wealth, profit, robes, and alms bowls, and further engaging in worldly affairs with householders—
by thus distancing oneself from this fiery pit, one can accomplish the supreme path.
Always delighting in subduing all demonic adversaries, Constantly turning the Wheel of Dharma to deliver all beings,
Thus extensively performing great benefit, One shall always meet virtuous friends and attain Bodhi.
Regarding kin and strangers, or blame and praise, they are always equal; the same applies to gain and loss, as well as envy.
Such unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddhas—those people will soon fully accomplish it all.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas that constitute dharmas of retributive suffering for bodhisattvas."
What are these four dharmas?

First, disparaging the teachings; second, clinging to the notions of self and person; third, lacking faith and understanding in the mind; and fourth, fully maintaining a fixed conviction regarding impure objects.
"These four dharmas constitute the conditions for the suffering retribution of a bodhisattva.
He further spoke in verse:
"If there is one who upholds the subtle and wondrous Dharma, They are worthy of receiving all the offerings of the world."
Those who treat others with contempt and lack great wisdom shall undergo boundless suffering from manifold evils;
those who constantly harbor notions of "person" and "self" toward the Buddha, their original teacher, and their parents,
and who do not seek such a mind of great merit, shall attain a state of impurity and ignorance.
The Triple Gem is the most supreme field of merit;
yet those who lack faith, understanding, and practice to offer their refuge and respect, being purely deceitful and deluded regarding the world, shall thus incur the suffering of evil karma.
Women are the gateway to the evil realms, wherein one wanders through birth and death without end.
Those who, out of ignorance and folly, perform such deeds, will sink forever into the hells and the animal realms.
But those who show reverence toward the Buddhas can extinguish all sufferings and attain fearlessness;
they close the gates to all evil destinies and lead sentient beings to the path of Buddhahood.
The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, Scroll One.
The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Dharma-transmitting Master, Your Servant Śīladharma, by Imperial Decree.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"There are four kinds of dharmas that act as fetters for bodhisattvas."
“What are these four dharmas?

First, treating others with contempt; second, seeking after worldly affairs through expedient means; third, a distracted mind that is like walking upon a perilous path; and fourth, single-minded attachment to one’s kinsmen.”
"These four dharmas constitute the fetters of a bodhisattva.
He further spoke in verse:
"If one acts with contempt toward others, And employs skillful means solely for worldly matters,"
Distraction is like walking upon a perilous path, or like an elephant with its body sunk deep in thick mud;
one gives rise to attachment for one's own kin, constantly harboring greedy longing as if intoxicated.
Thus entangled by various such bonds, delusion increases and covers great wisdom.
If a person fears suffering and loathes birth-and-death, seeking to escape the cycle of sinking to attain liberation,
and abandons worldly contempt and the like— this is called the path practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Having extinguished boundless sufferings, as well as their retinue of afflictions,
one attains ultimate peace and happiness with nothing further to seek, fulfilling the tranquil path of Bodhi.
Having fully perfected all virtues— such as the six perfections practiced, the three bodies, the five wisdoms,
and the ten powers— one is thus forever free from boundless suffering.
Having practiced for immeasurable eons in the past, you sought enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings;
you cultivated every kind of wholesome deed and remained far removed from all evil associates and the like.
Always delighting in deep mountains and secluded places, far removed from the perceptions of sound and form, one realizes true emptiness;
by thus practicing with unceasing diligence, one attains the perfect wisdom of a Great Man.
Beholding the conduct of sentient beings in this world, Whirling through the five realms of rebirth without end,
I gave rise to a heart of compassion in the past, Relinquishing my own life, wife, children, Kingdoms, cities,
the great earth, and precious treasures; Thus I sought Buddhahood for countless eons.
In the past, while I dwelt in the mountains practicing patience, the flowers, fruits, ponds, and marshes were all pure;
when King Kali came and severed my hands and feet, my mind gave rise to loving-kindness and forbearance, free from anger.
In the past, I dwelt in a deep mountain named Śama; I was then a seer named Bharadvāja.
At that time, a son of heaven shot my body with an arrow, yet I felt no anger or malice toward him.
I did not cherish my own life, regarding it as if it were a block of wood or stone, for my resolve to seek Bodhi never wavered.
In the past, when I was once a *sattva*, I saw a starving tigress about to devour her cubs;
I cast myself from a cliff to sacrifice my life and save them from hunger. Devas and humans praised my great diligence:
I always delight in practicing generosity to rescue sentient beings, Never begrudging my own body, life, or wealth.
In the past, I was once a Māṇava; I practiced extensive giving until the ocean of jewels was exhausted, relinquishing great maṇi-gems to enrich others, thus seeking to realize the fruit of Bodhi.
In the past, when I was King Mahāsoma, my fame for practicing the path was heard everywhere;
at that time, I entered bondage for the sake of others, thereby securing liberation for those hundred kings.
In the past, I was King Śakradatta, who fully satisfied all who made requests;
even my own body, life, and precious wealth were given so as to make others immensely wealthy and free from the suffering of poverty.
In the past, a flying pigeon came to seek refuge with me; I immediately cut flesh from my own body to save its life.
When I thus took up the knife and sliced the flesh, I was without alarm or fear, my mind remaining peaceful and composed.
In the past as well, he renounced his royal throne and practiced those pāramitās throughout his entire life;
furthermore, he manifested himself as a wondrous medicine, sacrificing his own body and life to save all living beings.
Furthermore, in the past he was once a lion king, Constantly acting for the benefit and happiness of the world;
Renouncing his royal throne and his retinue, He sought the unsurpassed path with single-minded resolve.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once King Sunakṣatra; at that time, he attained a lifespan of a thousand years.
For eighty-four years he practiced asceticism, exerting great diligence and bestowing precious wealth.
Before a Buddha stūpa, he ignited his own body, making an offering with a mind of sincere reverence.
Furthermore, in the past, when I was King Vimala, there was a Brahmin named Akṣimat who came to my inner palace and begged for my head;
I immediately relinquished my head and gave it to him as an offering.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once King Candraprabha, who universally rescued sentient beings and performed deeds of merit;
throughout all cities, fortresses, and villages, he distributed excellent medicines at the crossroads and along the highways.
A thousand women of exquisite and dignified beauty, adorned extensively with gold, jewels, and pearls—
renouncing those thousand women to practice the path oneself brings forth merit such as this that is beyond compare.
Furthermore, in the past he was King Śubha;
the precious crown he wore was rare in the world, adorned with fragrant flowers and various jewels, yet he gave it away to others without any stinginess.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once King Ratnaśikhin;
his hands and feet were as soft as tūla-cotton, fine, smooth, and subtle in color like a lotus, and he sacrificed his own hands and feet for the benefit of sentient beings.
Furthermore, in the past, when I was King An-yi, there was a merchant leader named Jing-he who,
leading a caravan of traders, sailed upon the great ocean and suddenly drifted down into the land of the rākṣasīs.
There were hundreds of thousands of yakṣī women there, shameless and extremely wicked, who fed solely on human flesh.
The merchants did not recognize them as yakṣīs; seeing their beauty, they conceived lustful thoughts.
Five hundred members of the caravan were about to be devoured, but I personally rescued them, and we all escaped the peril together.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once King Wondrous Eye, Constantly surrounded by four *koṭis* of women;
They were as upright and exquisite as celestial maidens, Yet he abandoned them, left the home life, and sought the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once King Puṇyaprabha, With stainless, pure, golden-colored skin;
his fingers were long and slender, rare in this world, Yet he gave away these fingers to benefit all living beings.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once King Dharmadatta; his deep blue eyes were as pure as the blue lotus.
Though it was his own body, the most difficult thing to relinquish, he gave it away to anyone who came to ask for it.
Furthermore, in the past, I was once King Padmanetra;
seeing sentient beings suffering in affliction, there was at that time a woman grieving with illness, whom I moved by compassion to liberate.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once a great king of physicians, Constantly rescuing all sentient beings suffering from illness;
Whether giving his own blood, marrow, or brain, He treated their diseases until they were healed.
With such a mind of courageous and diligent effort, He never for a moment abandoned living beings.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once King Chengli;
with his own beloved lotus-like eyes, he bestowed them upon sentient beings to heal their ailments, single-mindedly seeking the unsurpassed path.
Furthermore, in the past, he was a king named Samantadarśin, who out of compassion for sentient beings practiced their deliverance.
At that time, he gave away those four great continents, his kingdom, his subjects, and all manner of treasures—
even cutting from his own body flesh and blood— and bestowed them upon sentient beings with a joyful heart.
Furthermore, for the sake of the king’s daughter named Mahāprajñā, whose body was adorned with a golden hue and was soft and supple,
there was at that time a girl named Varṇalakṣaṇā; she was the daughter born to a merchant,
emaciated by hunger and suffering from a lack of food and drink, so I gave away both my breasts to save her life.
Furthermore, in the past, when he was a king named Bahusruta, all his precious jewels, exquisite garments,
elephants, horses, vehicles, wealth, silks, and so forth— such acts of giving were beyond counting.
Again I saw merchants adrift upon the ocean waves; I rescued them within the sea, yet they repaid my kindness with ingratitude by begging for my eyes;
I gave them to them as well, without a trace of anger.
Abandoning the great earth and all its retinue, he viewed them as unattached as an ant;
thus, in the past, he rescued sentient beings, his mind never wavering or succumbing to weariness.
Furthermore, seeing those who are solitary, aged, poor, or destitute, he provides them with all their necessities and serves them;
he constantly practices respect and affection without a mind of pride, and is free from shame or embarrassment, as well as from the notions of self and other.
Furthermore, in the past I once took the form of a monkey and traveled together with my kind;
at that time, encountering a hunter who bound his body, I immediately took his place so that he might escape death.
Thus, because I served the king, the king had the women of his harem bind me;
yet, thinking of my parents who were solitary and aged, I had no desire to eat any food or drink.
Enduring such suffering while cherishing filial devotion, I was therefore able to escape the perils of the royal palace.
Furthermore, in the past, he once took the form of a great bear; dwelling constantly in the deep mountains, he practiced compassion and patience.
Suddenly encountering a woodcutter caught in a heavy rain, he led him to a mountain cave to take shelter.
After these seven days had passed and the sky cleared, he told the woodcutter:
"Do not speak of me.
At that time, the woodcutter returned home in safety, but he lured hunters there to kill him.
Thus, though one who repays me with ingratitude has slain my body, I feel no anger or resentment, but give rise to loving-kindness and patience.
Furthermore, in the past, when I was a king of white elephants seeking the Bodhi of a Buddha and practicing the ten wholesome deeds, there was a hunter who shot my body;
I immediately cast away my tusks with a joyful heart.
In the past, there was an evil man named Dili who set fire to a great mountain wilderness;
seeing this fire, I exercised a mind of compassion, and the heavens rained down fragrant flowers so that the fire extinguished itself.
Furthermore, in the past, he was once a great king of deer, his body exquisitely adorned with gold and jewels;
entering that river, he rescued those drowning, enabling them to remain safe and whole in both body and life.
He said: "Do not say that I dwell in the mountains, for I fear those wicked men will come to hunt me down.
At that time, that man who had drowned turned his back on his benefactor's kindness and informed the king, leading him to capture me."
When my finger was severed, both my hands fell to the ground, yet at that time I felt not the slightest bit of anger.
Long ago, there was a company of five hundred merchants who set sail upon the great ocean in search of precious jewels;
the provisions of their leader were exhausted, and the merchant host grew hungry and emaciated for lack of food and drink.
At that time, I was the king of great tortoises; sacrificing my own body, I saved the lives of those merchants.
Because of my compassionate mind and desire to benefit others, we all reached the seashore in safety.
In the past, I transformed my body into a medicinal insect; this insect was named Kusuma.
All who suffered from disease ate of my body, and all obtained peace and freedom from ailment.
In the past, I was once a lion king, possessing great strength and fearlessness, practicing compassion;
when a great hunter shot my body, I felt neither resentment nor anger.
In the past, I was also a White Horse King, Constantly practicing the compassionate deeds of a Bodhisattva;
I rescued those merchants from the perils of the rākṣasas, Carrying all the people across the great ocean.
In the past, as the bird Gaṇḍaka, I remained far removed from sensual desire and free from distraction,
causing the flocks of birds of my own kind to likewise practice pure conduct.
Furthermore, in a former life as a king of rabbits, he proclaimed the practice of the Dharma to his flock;
seeing a seer who was hungry and had no food, he immediately sacrificed his own body to save that being's life.
Furthermore, in the past, I once took the form of a parrot, Dwelling constantly within groves of flowering fruit trees;
When wicked men came to destroy this forest, It flourished and grew lush once more through my power.
Furthermore, in the past, I was once a king of monkeys, wandering together with a great multitude of monkeys.
At that time, a king came to capture them; I rescued them from their peril by appearing before the king.
Furthermore, in the past, I was once a parrot; my parents were both old and lacked the strength to fly.
I would carry grains of rice from the fields in my beak to nourish my two parents and practice filial piety.
Thereupon the field-owner, harboring a fit of rage, seized the parrot and rebuked him:
"How can you steal my rice?
At this moment, I must see you give up your life!"
The parrot said to the field owner:
"The field you have sown provides for all; I take but a small portion to support my two parents.
Why do you say that I am a thief?"
At that time, the landowner, hearing these words, was filled with even greater joy and gave him double the amount of rice, saying:
"I am a bird and you are a human; such filial devotion has never been seen before."
In the past, when practicing the bodhisattva path, You traversed countless eons as numerous as atoms;
Seeking to attain the great enlightenment of Buddhahood, You never felt even a moment of weariness.
Thus, having extensively practiced these perfections— giving away internal and external wealth, kingdoms, cities, wives,
children, and precious jewels, as well as one's head, eyes, marrow, brain, and even life itself; and practicing morality, patience, diligence,
meditation, wisdom, skillful means, vows, and powers— Thus, having extensively practiced these various perfections,
Never for a moment did they abandon the bodhisattva practices, nor was any of all their wholesome deeds left behind.
Just as the Buddha taught the dhūta ascetic practices, those practices were also undertaken as causes for attaining Buddhahood;
thus, each and every one was cultivated to completion, practicing with diligence and without transgression.
In the final age of the future, there will be sentient beings who, though having become bhikṣus, lack the conduct of the Saṃgha;
constantly giving rise to pride and indolence, they are greedily attached to sounds, forms, and material gain.
Upon hearing this supreme and wondrous cause of great practice, they instead respond with slander and refuse to believe or accept it.
Laughing lightly, he addressed the people with these words:
"What has been taught here is not the Buddha's teaching.
I have heard that in the past there was a man, learned and well-versed in the sciences, who was named Sāgara."
Hearing what the Buddha has taught, they do not believe or accept it, but instead question their own teachers about these words of the Dharma.
Those teachers, though aged and themselves well-versed in learning, likewise do not believe these words of the Buddha;
thus, they pass the matter on in this manner to others:
"There is no self, no person, and no sentient being; this teaching is not the true instruction.
To undergo toil in vain seeking liberation—were one to thus maintain the precepts and train in dignified conduct, for what purpose would such cultivation be?"

Since there are no sentient beings, no self, and no person, And even parents and kinsmen do not exist, These are the words of heterodox paths with false views; They are not the Dharma of true liberation.
Furthermore, in the final age, there will be bhikṣus who commit various transgressions without shame or remorse;
with pride, arrogance, and distracted minds, they burn with hatred, envy, greed, and attachment as if by fire.
Wearing the three robes untidily, they walk with hands hanging down;
trailing their saṃghāṭī robes as they enter the village, they indulge in sensual pleasures and drink wine, engaging in all manner of coarse and evil conduct.
Clad in the dharma robes as a messenger of the Buddha, yet not relying on the precepts while drawing near to kings and lords;
rushing about on errands and delivering letters to the four quarters, they rely on official power to seek wealth and profit;
thus they fall away from the grove of the Tathāgata’s merit and virtue, descending into the three miserable realms and various evil destinies.
Some may engage in business at market stalls, while others may live in villages farming;
the Buddha said:
"Such as these are not śramaṇas; pure bhikṣus should not associate with them."
They constantly misappropriate the wealth and offerings of the Sangha as if it were their own;
seeing virtuous bhikṣus, they give rise to arrogance and slander them.
Deluded and ignorant, they violate the code of discipline and secretly engage in defiled and depraved conduct within the homes of the laity.
They maintain wives and children, engaging in all manner of worldly affairs; they act with coarse and evil conduct, no different from the laity.
By thus extensively creating the causes of unwholesome karma, they fail to follow the path of a renunciant śramaṇa.
They shall fall into the three miserable realms and evil destinies, sinking for eternal kalpas to undergo manifold sufferings.
Failing to discipline one's own faculties, and being greedily attached to food and sensual desire, one is constantly held in contempt by others;
the same is true for the disciples one has trained.
Never having been instructed in the methods of practice, nor possessing a heart of reverence for teacher and disciple,
they speak of themselves as compassionate before others, not out of a desire for their students to practice service and attendance.
Some may suffer from wind-disorders or leprosy, or be ugly people with impaired faculties;
even if such as these are accepted and ordained, they are not true śramaṇas or disciples of the Buddha.
Those who have no precepts, no conduct, and no virtue—neither laypeople nor śramaṇas—are like one carrying firewood to burn a putrid corpse; those who are pure should keep them at a distance.
By nature one is inherently restless and prone to great distraction, like a wild elephant that has lost its training;
even dwelling in deep mountains, the mind finds no peace, as the fire of craving burns without a moment’s rest.
Forgetting all the virtues of the Buddhas— skillful means, wisdom, and the dhūta practices—
and failing to practice any such wholesome deeds, they fall into the great Avīci hell from which there is no escape.
They constantly discourse within cities, towns, and villages on matters of state, bandits, and kin;
thus they contemplate these things day and night, never for even a moment practicing samādhi.
Furthermore, conceiving greed for the vihāra, they extensively construct courtyards, halls, and dwellings;
entirely devoid of recitation or ascetic practice, they do so only for the sake of their kin and disciples.
If there are bhikṣus who rely upon me, I shall dwell together with you;
if you wish to uphold the precepts and observe the disciplinary code, that which is not my way must be kept at a distance.
All bedding, couches, and the like, as well as household utensils, articles of enjoyment, and food and drink—
having hidden them away in a deep inner room and concealed them—
one says: "There is nothing at all."
"Having caused others to depart, such foolish people in the final age will cause the Buddha's teachings to perish before long.
Greedily seeking gain and offerings, they sever their roots of goodness; such bhikṣus are exceedingly numerous.
If there are those with pure wisdom, they should distance themselves from them and dwell in deep mountains."
In the age of the Final Dharma, bhikṣus lack the virtue of the precepts;

They take no pleasure in dwelling in the deep mountains in silent seclusion, But constantly reside within royal cities and market towns, Devoting themselves solely to matters of right and wrong and to strife and contention.
Consequently, they are restrained by the laws of the king, Subjected to rebukes and scoldings, driven out and banished, And forced to endure shame and humiliation.
The ocean of merit of the Buddhas' Dharma teachings is entirely dried up by those who break the precepts.
It is like the precious waters of the sea, pure and clear, yet becoming turbid when covered by mud;
or like lotuses blooming in full bloom across a pond, yet being destroyed by a violent wind.
Thus it is with those who break the precepts during the age of the Dharma’s decay; they likewise cause the decline of the Buddha’s teachings.
If there are those who purely cultivate the holy life, they should always distance themselves from such evil friends when encountering them.
When the lives of such people end, they fall into Avīci Hell, where they undergo suffering for hundreds of thousands of countless eons.
After having undergone punishment in this hell, one may be reborn among animals or as a human; yet one will be impoverished,
low-born, deaf, mute, one-eyed, stunted, ugly, and afflicted by many diseases,
with hands, feet, and sense organs incomplete— such that all who see one are struck with terror.
Lacking faith, lacking practice, and lacking roots of goodness, they suffer constant anxiety and distress from hunger and cold day and night;
furthermore, they are met with the resentment of others, who strike them with tiles and stones.
Thus, constantly bound by these three sufferings, one should distance oneself from all sinful karma;
one must always draw near to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and purely uphold the precepts and the dhūta practices.
Thus fame, profit, and one's retinue are like illusions, like transformations, like reflections;
conditioned phenomena are but momentary, soon to be separated from and then disintegrate.

Only the unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi, the wondrous ground, the ten powers, and the pāramitās—cultivate these with firm resolve and do not give rise to doubt; in the future, there will be ultimate great peace and bliss.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:

"If there is a person who does not practice in accordance with the Dharma regarding the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and possesses such faults, they will be respected and loved by those who likewise do not practice in accordance with the Dharma; the indolent will be respected and loved by the indolent, and the ignorant will be respected and loved by the ignorant."

In this way, they harbor mutual affection and attachment for gain and offerings; they are jealous of the noble; they are indolent and deranged; they engage in frivolous speech and double-tongued slander; they flatter others with sycophancy; and they deceive their parents as well as their own teachers.
"Or, entering royal cities and various villages, they do not transform the multitudes for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, but instead speak exclusively in falsehoods:
'I am of great wisdom, widely learned and erudite.'"

Deceiving and deluding sentient beings while seeking only wealth and profit, they utterly abandon the wholesome Dharma and gain nothing at all; they are like a broken vessel, incapable of holding or being used.

They harbor much resentment and malice toward the multitude, listening to and believing false words, and through empty and false speculations, they declare what is Dharma to be non-Dharma and what is non-Dharma to be Dharma, having no heart of love or joy for the Buddha’s true Dharma.

Born into a low-born and impoverished family, he entered the Buddha-dharma for the sake of meager gain; hoping to seek ordination and become a monk, he practiced unchaste conduct and achieved nothing at all within the teachings of the Buddha-dharma, let alone great wisdom.
The Buddha told the Venerable One:
"A person such as this should not preach the Dharma.
Since they cannot even sustain the wholesome roots of humans and devas, how much less could they achieve the realization of Bodhi?"
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:
"There are eight kinds of individuals who are far removed from enlightenment; for them, the sublime Dharma should not be preached."
Rāṣṭrapāla said:
"What are these eight kinds of persons?
I only pray that you will explain them."
The Buddha said:
"First, one is born there among the mlecchas;
second, one is born there into a poor family."
Third, one will take birth in a lowly and base family;
fourth, even if one obtains a human body, it will be ugly, deformed, dull, and stupid;
fifth, one will be fully possessed by the hindrances and entanglements, with body and mind filled with sorrow and distress.
Sixth, they turn their backs on the worthy and good, and associate with evil friends;
seventh, they suffer from chronic illness, their bodies becoming frail and emaciated;
eighth, they are oppressed by manifold sufferings until the end of their lives.
"These eight kinds of individuals are far removed from enlightenment and are not permitted to preach the Dharma.
Thereupon, Rāṣṭrapāla again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What further meaning is there in their not being permitted to preach the Dharma?"
The Buddha said: “Rāṣṭrapāla!
If there were a person (pudgala) who lacked decisiveness, I would not speak of awakening (bodhi).”
To those who are deluded by falsehood, I do not speak of pure conduct;
to those who are indolent, I do not speak of the bodhisattva path;
to those who are stingy, I do not speak of the practice of making offerings to the Buddha.
To those possessed of the conceit of "I," I do not speak of the purity of the perfections;
to those lacking wisdom, I do not speak of the dharma that severs doubt;
to those who are envious, I do not speak of the purity of the mind.
To those who lack the faculty of faith, I do not teach the dharma of dhāraṇī;
to those who lack virtue, I do not teach the dharma of the Sugata;
to those who are greedy for affection, I do not teach the purity of the body.
To those who possess unwholesome restraint, I do not speak of the dharma that the Buddha has faults;
to those who engage in false speech, I do not speak of purity of speech;
to those who harbor pride, I do not speak of the dharma of reverence.
To those who lack understanding, I do not speak of the dharmas of training;
to those who act solely for the sake of body and life, I do not speak of seeking the dharma of the Path.
Such individuals as these should not be taught the Dharma.
Then Rakṣapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What do you think?
The Buddha said:
“Rāṣṭrapāla!

For the sake of these sentient beings who are deluded by ignorance, whose consciousnesses are inverted, who engage in false conceptualization, and who do not rely on the teachings of the Dharma—even for those among gods and humans—you should not speak of this.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Uncertain are all sentient beings, Such as *pudgalas* and the like;
Arrogant with the conceit of self, They are greedily attached to gain and offerings.”
Constantly practicing non-restraint, deeply attached to the five desires,
they increase all afflictions and remain far removed from the Buddha’s bodhi.
They fall away from wholesome dharmas, being indolent and failing to practice.
Full of hesitation and much distraction, they do not give rise to faith or acceptance regarding the words of the Dharma of the precepts.
Though they employ skillful means to seek renunciation, even if they succeed in becoming bhikṣus, [they remain thus].
Lightly abandoning the path of the Dharma, like discarding a load of gold and jewels to carry a load of hemp,
one reaches that place of tranquility, yet has no intention to delight in the practice of meditation.
With perverse thoughts and distracted minds, they obstruct eloquence and sink into great ignorance; they fall into the evil realms.
Even if they should obtain a human body, it will be ugly and incomplete.
Lax in nature and deluded, they do not practice the various wholesome dharmas.
Their faculties are perpetually dark and dull;
they fall into great perils and difficulties, wandering for millions of kalpas, lost and unable to attain liberation.
If one could realize the Buddha’s bodhi by practicing perverted means of benefiting others,
then Devadatta— who lacked right knowledge— would have attained the fruit of a Sugata.
If a person, out of greed for gain and offerings, causes sentient beings to fall into ruin, [they will surely suffer the same].
Just as the great power of the wind in the sky can cause all flying birds to fall,
so too is the meaning when the force of one’s improper merit is exhausted.
Those who lack faith and violate the precepts are like the blind when they behold the wholesome.
Just as funeral wood for cremation is shunned by those who dislike inauspiciousness,
so too, though one may give rise to a virtuous mind,
if one lacks that vast wisdom and slanders the Dharma out of lack of faith, liberation will not be ultimate.
For example, like a painting without glue, the colors of its adornment will not last long;
so too is the meaning of one who is conceited with self-pride.
If one seeks the Buddha’s bodhi, one should not begrudge even body or life.
Regarding the words of the profound Dharma, one should courageously and diligently practice and study them.
Abandoning wholesome conduct and practicing what is unrighteous, one’s actions increase faults and cause one to fall into a great pit of fire.
Receiving and practicing according to the Dharma, severing all craving and attachment,
and cultivating the roots of myriad virtues; even regarding a single phrase,
they attain thorough penetration and complete understanding— thus they accumulate merit.
“Having accomplished the supreme path, one is forever freed from ignorance and blindness.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:

“In the past, through immeasurable, boundless, unspeakably unspeakable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Siddhārthamati Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
"At that time, there was a great king named Prabhāsa who ruled over Jambudvīpa; his territory was sixteen thousand yojanas in extent, and within it were twenty thousand cities and towns."

The city where King Prabhāsa resided was named Ratnaprabhā; the city was twelve yojanas long from east to west and seven yojanas wide from south to north, and it was composed of the seven precious jewels in seven concentric tiers.
That king practiced the Eightfold Noble Path; his lineage was noble and flourishing with a thousand koṭis of members, and the people of that country lived for ten koṭis of years.
The king had a crown prince named Puṇyaprabha, who possessed all his faculties, was handsome and dignified in appearance, and was foremost in exquisite beauty.

At the time of the Prince’s birth, a thousand treasure troves surged forth from the earth—one of these appeared before the royal palace, filled with the seven precious gems and reaching a height of seven men. Furthermore, it caused all sentient beings to have their every wish fulfilled, even those who were bound in fetters attained liberation.

Furthermore, seven days after that great prince was born, he attained complete mastery in all arts, crafts, and mathematics; indeed, there were no worldly or supramundane undertakings that he did not thoroughly understand.
"During the night, the Devaputra Pure Light came to preach the Dharma for him, saying to the Prince:
'Bhagavān Puṇyaprabha, listen attentively!
You must quiet your mind; you should not be distracted, and you should always remain far removed from all sensory objects.'"

Day and night one should contemplate conditioned phenomena, observing their impermanence; when life comes to an end, who is there to save? Thus, one should give rise to fear toward all that is unrighteous.

yet through courageous and diligent practice, until the end of one's life,

He feels no attachment to any gardens, groves, flowers, streams, bathing pools, songs, dances, or musical performances in the world; he completely distances himself from all desired things, including kingdoms, cities, palaces, elephants, horses, carriages, gold, silver, wealth, and treasures.
With single-minded contemplation, he thought:
"My body is illusory, a mere temporary conglomeration of the four elements; it possesses no solidity or substance. The great earth and all the heavens are likewise not ultimate."

Ordinary beings constantly engage in unrighteousness; deluded by ignorance, they discriminate between kin and strangers, indulging in sensual pleasures without satiety, remaining forever in saṃsāra with no time of liberation.
"I have taken birth among such deluded and confused people.
