"King Prabhāsa selected the most supreme, pure, and wondrous auspicious site for his crown prince and constructed a city there named Priyaṃkara.
That city had sevenfold walls; within it were seven hundred streets, all of which were completely covered with nets of bells, pearls, and the seven precious gems."

Furthermore, there were sixty thousand exquisite canopies made of various jewels and eighty thousand jeweled banners arranged in succession throughout the streets and alleys. Each jeweled banner was adorned with sixty thousand jeweled cords, and each jeweled cord possessed fourteen *koṭis* of musical instruments. When stirred by a gentle breeze, these instruments produced exquisite sounds like those of hundreds of thousands of celestial concerts.

Furthermore, in every street, lane, and thoroughfare of this city, five hundred young maidens dwell; these maidens are of exquisite physical form and countenance, their features are serene and pleasing, and they are fully capable of all forms of music, song, dance, and performance.
Then King Prabhāsa issued a decree, saying:
"Let all the young maidens perform music day and night without interruption.

He commanded that all the people from the four quarters who entered this city, upon seeing such music and scenes of joy, should flock together to watch and enjoy them, thereby causing the Prince’s heart to become attached to pleasure.

Furthermore, the King said: "To all sentient beings who seek food and drink, I shall give food and drink; to those who seek clothing, I shall give clothing; to those who seek flower garlands and unguents, I shall give flower garlands and unguents; to those who seek beds, couches, and bedding, I shall give beds, couches, and bedding. Even unto gold, silver, mani-jewels, tridacna shells, agate, coral, pearls, and lapis lazuli—such various treasures shall be heaped up everywhere. Moreover, there shall be elephants, horses, and carriages, all adorned with various kinds of precious gems, so that all sentient beings may enjoy them as they please."

At that time, King Prabhāsa further constructed a palace for the crown prince within this city, one yojana in width. He built four gate-towers, and all the doors, windows, and balconies were adorned with various kinds of the seven treasures.

Within this palace, he established a great hall adorned on all sides with hundreds of thousands of rare jewels; in the center of the hall, he placed four *koṭi* of couches and bedding made of various precious gems.
Furthermore, within the city, he established a great garden where flowers, fruits, and trees were so numerous that they grew lushly and blossomed in profusion, a sight rarely seen in the world.
Within that space, all jewel trees were arranged, their radiance shining so brightly that there was nothing not delightful.
Furthermore, within the garden were ponds made of the seven treasures; on the four sides of each pond were four boundary paths composed of four jewels, namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
One hundred and eight lion mouths were placed around the perimeter of the pond for the water to enter through them;
another one hundred and eight lion mouths were placed [around it] for the water to exit through them.
Within it, furthermore, various kinds of famous flowers—such as the *padma*, *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—are constantly in full bloom all around the perimeter of the pond.

Furthermore, there were eight hundred jewel trees; upon each jewel tree hung precious cords, and upon each cord were tens of millions of musical instruments. When stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced exquisite sounds that caused all sentient beings who heard them to feel joy and delight.

Furthermore, the precious trees were hung with eight million exquisite banners made of rare jewels, and a great jeweled net was placed over the pond as a canopy to cover the Prince’s body and keep it free from dust and dirt.

"At that time, King Prabhāsa further ordered that within the palace four *koṭi* of thrones be fashioned from the seven precious gems; upon each throne, five hundred exquisite and superior garments were spread."

In the midst of this, a great throne was placed, seven men in height, upon which eighty koṭis of exquisite, superior jewel-garments were spread; this was the throne upon which Prince Puṇyaprabha ascended.

Before each of the seats, incense burners made of pure gold were placed; around the perimeter of each burner hung golden bells and golden lotuses, while nets of *maṇi* jewels adorned the four sides, radiating brilliant light. Day and night, during the three periods, they constantly burned aloeswood incense and scattered exquisite flowers.
Furthermore, within the garden there were nine million nine hundred thousand mani jewels; each mani jewel was one yojana in width and emitted a great radiance that illuminated all worlds.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:

"Within the pleasure grove of Prince Puṇyaprabha there are various kinds of flying birds, such as parrots, mynas, mandarin ducks, geese, ducks, peacocks, śāris, kokilas, kroñcas, kalaviṅkas, kalaviṅkas, and jīvajīvakas."

Thus, these various birds all speak with the voices of virtuous people; whenever they fly in flocks, they produce subtle and wondrous sounds—no different from a symphony of many musical instruments—and like the Garden of Joy belonging to the Lord of Devas, they cause all devas and humans to experience sublime bliss.
That Devaputra Prabhāsa further prepared exquisite, superior food and drink for the Crown Prince, providing five hundred thousand carts of it every day.

Furthermore, he dispatched envoys to various cities and villages to select young maidens—between sixteen and twenty years of age—who were of beautiful appearance and perfect physical features; who were neither too tall nor too short, neither too stout nor too thin, and neither too fair nor too dark; whose bodies exhaled the fragrance of white sandalwood and whose mouths the scent of the *utpala* lotus; whose speech was elegant and refined, whose minds were pure and straightforward and free from jealousy; and who were skilled in games of chance and skill, singing, dancing, and entertainment, indeed proficient in all worldly crafts and arts. Thus, eighty *koṭis* of such maidens arrived and entered the royal city.

"At that time, the Devaputra Prabhāsa bestowed these eighty koṭis of maidens upon the Prince; the King himself bestowed all the maidens from his own palace, totaling one koṭi; the King’s kinsmen and relatives also presented one koṭi of maidens to the Prince; the high ministers and chief counselors likewise presented one koṭi of maidens to the Prince; and the commoners of the capital city also presented one koṭi of maidens to the Prince. Thus, eighty-four koṭis of maidens were all made to attend upon and serve him, providing entertainment through song, dance, and music to delight the Prince."
The Buddha said to the Venerable Rakṣita:

"At that time, having witnessed these things, Prince Puṇyaprabha felt no attachment whatsoever toward his royal city, palaces, towers, pavilions, gardens, groves, ponds, elephants, horses, precious jewels, nor toward the various entertainments such as the maidens, singing, dancing, and musical performances."
He then reflected to himself:

"These women have become great evil friends to me; they sever my roots of goodness and increase my afflictions. I shall dwell perpetually in saṃsāra without autonomy, just as a person caught in captivity can never escape."

At that time, having perceived these faults, for ten years the Prince did not become attached to the five sensory objects—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. With a single-minded focus, he reflected:
"How may I abandon these evil companions and practice by myself to attain liberation?"
Having had this thought, those young maidens went immediately to the royal palace and said to their father, the king:
"Prince Puṇyaprabha pays no heed whatsoever to the court ladies, nor to games, pleasures, singing, or dancing; he sits alone in contemplation, remaining far removed from sounds and sights."
At that time, having heard these words, the Devaputra Prabhāsa was suddenly struck with alarm and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Immediately, leading eighty thousand minor kings and various ministers, he entered the palace where the Prince resided. There he saw the Prince dwelling alone in the palace, his countenance serene yet shedding tears in sorrowful weeping; his heart was filled with great anguish, and he fainted and fell to the ground, regaining consciousness only after a long while.
Rising from the ground, he immediately spoke in verse:
"A son is the most supreme treasure; why do you not look upon me?
My mind is distressed and agitated with grief."
How can one renounce all that is beloved— the various forms of wealth and pleasure?
Adorned with manifold jewels, there are palaces and exquisite pavilions,
gardens and bathing pools, as well as elephants, horses, and the seven kinds of precious treasures.
With garments and food and drink, in such infinite quantities,

Like those celestial maidens,
she mastered all the arts— song, dance, and music—

That which was intended to please you and bring joy to your heart—
having abandoned that, why do you dwell alone in the deep palace with such a profoundly serene countenance?
Each harboring grief and distress, like withered lotuses,

Such were these young maidens, all upright and youthful;
from their mouths issued the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and their bodies bore the scent of sandalwood.

"Throughout day and night, you have been close to me in playful enjoyment.
Now that this very time has come, you abandon me here.
What do you think?"
Please explain this to me quickly.
Furthermore, within the groves, ninety-nine hundred thousand mani-jewels have been placed, each one yojana in width.

There dwell many kinds of flying birds: peacocks, geese, ducks, and more.
Kalaviṅkas, parrot-finch birds, and others, all produce subtle and wondrous sounds.
Furthermore, among the various trees, precious cords hang down from each;
within every one of these precious cords, there are exquisite musical instruments.
When a gentle breeze stirs them, they emit wondrous sounds;
their clear resonance is like celestial music—how could one not cherish this?
Furthermore, these various palaces are all constructed from myriad jewels.
Gold, silver, mani-jewels, Mother-of-pearl and agate,
Lapis lazuli, pearls, and so forth— Their adornments are most subtle and wondrous.
Within this precious hall, a fragrant incense burner was installed;
pearl nets hung down on all four sides, and ten million exquisite,
fine garments were used to adorn its summit.
Constantly burning sandalwood incense, it is no different from the Hall of Good Dharma in the palace of Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Yet they turn their backs on their parents, possessing not a single heart of filial piety or reverence.

Having said this, she wept with grief:
"Please explain it to me quickly!"
Upon seeing what was asked, the Prince bowed his head and addressed his father,
the King: "Falling into the state of sentient beings, bound by the fetters of living creatures,
increasing great faults, and dwelling forever in saṃsāra."
There is no way to attain liberation through them.
Now, seeking deliverance, I have resolved upon the great bodhicitta and remain far removed from all defilements.
The bodies of all women are the source of manifold evils and impurities.
I view them as enemies;
wandering through birth and death, they bind all sentient beings,
who constantly dwell upon a great and perilous path.
The skin envelops impurities— blood, flesh, bones, marrow,
intestines, stomach, feces, urine, sweat, tears, mucus, saliva, and the like.
How can one find delight in such a foul and loathsome body?
It is like a poisonous tree whose blossoms are beloved by all;
yet when one gathers its flowers, the poison enters the body, and before one realizes it, its life is extinguished.
So too are the kingdom and the city, the palace, the music, and the songs and dances.
Ultimately they are not solid, like dreams or magical illusions.
They are also like trees in spring, lush with foliage and fragrant;
yet when winter arrives, they wither and fall away, all becoming parched and decayed.
Women and wealth likewise do not endure for long.
With minds deluded and deranged by folly, they are constantly submerged in the ocean of craving;
giving rise to strife, hatred, and jealousy, they perpetrate mutual slaughter.
Father the king and his retinue, wife and children, both male and female—
who among them could provide rescue within those evil realms?
Only the Bodhisattva, a person of great wisdom, whose body and mind are ever tranquil.
Regard them as mere grass and wood; remain unmoving like Mount Sumeru.
Always delight in dwelling in deep mountains, seeking the True Path with a single mind.
This floating world does not endure for long, like a swift torrent of mountain water.
Human life is like a drifting cloud; in an instant it disperses and vanishes.
One falls into the three realms of existence, lost and submerged in birth and death.
I do not cling to folly or delusion, but remain far removed from all that is false and illusory.
Forms, sounds, and the five objects of desire are not the domain of a bodhisattva.
When merit is exhausted, demerit arises; when karma is exhausted, karma is born again.
Like a bird confined within a cage, one never attains true autonomy.
The six sense objects are like venomous snakes, Inflicting harm and distress upon sentient beings;
The four great elements are not solid or real, Like an empty village.
O Father King, you should now know this:
Taking refuge in true liberation, you constantly ply the wondrous Dharma-boat to deliver beings from the three realms of existence.
You grant release from the bonds of restraint, and cause those afflicted by suffering to attain peace.
Granting sight to the blind, bestowing precious wealth upon the poor,
causing all to be free from sorrow and suffering;
drying up the river of craving and illuminating the path through darkness.
Pervading like clouds and thunder, he pours down a rain of ambrosia;
removing heat and attaining coolness, he achieves supreme wisdom.
Father King, you should now know this:
Who, harboring loving-kindness and patience, would wish to become an enemy?
Who, endowed with wisdom, would fear the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
Who, possessing eyes, would enter upon a perilous path?
Who, having attained Bodhi, would wish to create distraction?
A person of such wisdom will certainly not travel by a deviant path.
Though he cast himself into the great ocean, he never gave rise to defiled attachment for these five sensual desires;
nor did he feel such toward his kinsmen— please, Your Majesty, have him brought back at once.
Do not dwell here for long;
the household life has many faults that obscure the Buddha’s bodhi, as do its various attendants. Depart instead for the deep mountains.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:

"That Prince Puṇyaprabha was situated within the precious palace, surrounded and attended by these young maidens. Upon observing them, the prince felt a profound sense of weary detachment; while moving through the three dignified postures of walking, standing, and sitting, he sought to sever all afflictions."
On the eighth day of the month, he sat upon the ground and correctly contemplated, free from all worldly defilements.
Having performed this contemplation, during the middle watch of the night, he suddenly heard the Pure Light Deva King in the air praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the community of bhikṣus.
Having heard this, the hairs on his body stood on end; with grief and joy mingling together, he joined his palms toward the sky and asked in verse:
"O Greatly Compassionate Devas of the void, Who is it that you have praised by raising your voices?"
"I seek refuge and long for liberation; I pray that you will joyfully grant me an exposition.
At that time, the Devaputra Pure Light (Vimalaprabha), hearing those questions from within the void, spoke of the matters worthy of praise for the Prince, answering him in verse:
"I now extol the Great Śramaṇa; that Buddha is named Arthasiddhamati."
He constantly transforms the deluded multitudes with the ten wholesome paths, rescuing the orphaned, the solitary, and all who suffer.
Skillful means and wisdom are his supreme qualities; his merit and spiritual power are beyond compare.
There are always ten thousand nayutas of bhikṣus who constantly pay him homage.
The Prince again asked the Pure Light Deva:
"What are his merits and marks of excellence?
Please explain once more for me, as I wish to hear, the bodhisattva practices performed by that Buddha."
At that time, the Devaputra Pure Light (Vimalaprabha) further explained the Buddha’s merits and marks of physical excellence to the Prince, responding in verse:
“The Buddha’s crown is like Mount Sumeru, Rising high and prominent above the multitude;
His conch-like hair is deep azure, Whirling to the right, all perfectly uniform.”
The white tuft of hair between his brows radiates light, brilliant as a thousand suns;
his eyes are deep blue and clear, like the petals of a blue lotus;
his jaw and chest are like those of a lion, and the color of his lips surpasses that of the *bimba* fruit.
His teeth are closely set without gaps or loss, white like white jade or snow;
his navel is broad and spirals to the right, like a pure lapis lazuli gem;
his tongue is the color of a red lotus, broad, long, thin, and pure.
The wheel-mark upon his forehead is broad and expansive; this sign is most subtle and wondrous.
His Brahma-voice is clear and resonant, exquisite and transcending the world;
all devas and humans who hear it are filled with joy.
Even if there were hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, none could equal the Buddha’s voice;
its merit is vast and boundless, able to sever the delusions of sentient beings and cause them to practice the path to enlightenment.
Known as kinnaras, ruddy sheldrakes, cuckoos, varhiṇas, geese, krauñcas, kunālas,
kalaviṅkas, and kalaviṅkas— each adorned with their own distinct physical forms;
The Buddha’s marks and signs are likewise so.
With but a single word, the Buddha causes each member of the assembly to attain understanding; near and far, all hear him equally.
The Tathāgata possesses mastery over the Dharma, his neck long, slender, and exquisite.
His proportions are equal to his limbs;
with his hands hanging down, they reach past his knees. Thus he is wondrously and exquisitely adorned, with all seven parts of his body being level and full.
His two arms are like the trunks of elephants; his two calves surpass those of the king of deer;
his private organ is concealed within a sheath, just like that of a noble steed;
the hairs on his body are deep blue and curl to the right; and he is as fearless as a lion.
The Buddha’s crown is like a celestial canopy, his golden body adorned with majesty;
his feet display the thousand-spoked wheel and the *śaśāṅka* mark.
Thus, in such vast and sublime dignity, he is exceedingly rare in the world.
If you now draw near to those who possess virtue and those who lack it,
those with merit and those without, you shall come to know each one for yourself.
If one invokes the name of the Buddha, they remain unattached to both praise and blame.
"Just as a lotus in the water cannot be defiled by the mud,
so too is our Buddha, the Great Guide, unsurpassed in the world.
Thus ends the third fascicle of the *Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla*.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Dharma-transmitting Master, Your Servant Shi Hu, respectfully translates by imperial decree: The Buddha addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:

"At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha heard the Devaputra Viśuddhaprabha in the void praising the immeasurable merits of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, as well as their marks, signs, and adornments; his heart was filled with great joy."
With right intention and focused mind, he sat upright and reflected:
"That Buddha, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with merit; the sublime Dharma he teaches is true and without error; and his śrāvaka disciples maintain pure and stainless holy conduct."
He further reflected:

"Samsara is great suffering; all sentient beings are obscured by ignorance, failing to perceive or understand, and constantly giving rise to various defilements through the view of a self-body, thereby extensively increasing their faults. The cycle of birth and death continues without interruption; those with wisdom should distance themselves from it."
Again, he reflected:

"Deluded by ignorance and darkness, three kinds of volitional formations arise—those that initiate body and speech, those that create wholesome and unwholesome karma, and those that perfume consciousness to form seeds. In this way, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling continue in succession as the retribution of suffering; craving and grasping entangle and moisten them, causing the link of existence to grow."
In this way, there is rebirth-linking, old age, and death.
Who can escape them?
I contemplate that birth and death have little flavor and much suffering, and they oppress both body and mind; they are to be reviled and dreaded.
You should quickly draw near to that Buddha and the subtle, wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata, severing all afflictions and seeking deliverance from saṃsāra.
If you associate with evil friends and indulge in sensual pleasures, you will not even attain the rewards of humans or devas, let alone Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, having formed this thought, Prince Puṇyaprabha conceived a deep sense of weary detachment toward this palace city:
"I shall never attain liberation here; it is fitting that I quickly abandon this place and seek a secluded spot to practice the holy life."

When the prince had formed this resolve, he immediately left the palace and intended to go out through the gate; yet, fearing that his kinsmen might obstruct him, he returned to the hall, stood facing east, and addressed the Buddha from afar:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Chengyi possesses all-encompassing wisdom and vast supernormal powers."
"I pray that you grant me your compassionate protection; I shall cast my body from this place to seek liberation.

Having spoken these words, he immediately threw himself down. The Buddha, by means of his supernormal power, extended his right hand and emitted a great radiance that illuminated the Prince’s body; the light transformed into a thousand-petaled lotus flower that received the Prince’s feet.

Furthermore, this lotus emitted hundreds of thousands of subtle and wondrous rays of light that illuminated the Prince, causing his heart to feel serene joy; in a mere moment, he was brought before the Buddha.
The Buddha withdrew his radiance, and the lotuses disappeared.

At that time, the prince descended like a mountain descending, and upon reaching the presence of the Buddha, he joined his palms in reverence, circumambulated the World-Honored One, and with a sincere heart, recited:
"Namo to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Siṃhaghoṣa; I take refuge in the sublime Dharma taught by him and the assembly of bhikṣus."
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself on the ground before the Buddha, performing a thousand bows, and praised the Buddha with this verse:
"I bow my head to the Unsurpassed Great King of Physicians; The great affliction of my body has long remained uncured.
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will grant me deliverance, And bestow upon me a small measure of the Tathāgata’s wondrous medicinal Dharma."
Sitting alone day and night in self-reflection, he single-mindedly sought liberation from the realm of the five desires.
Then, a celestial being from the empty realm raised his voice, exhorting him to take refuge and come to the Buddha’s presence.
The Buddha is the Great Teacher who has appeared in the world; how could sentient beings fail to commit transgressions?
Within great calamities, he extends his protection and salvation, causing those who are blind and deluded to open the eye of wisdom.
Although I have now given rise to a mind of faith in the Buddha, I am destitute of the jewels of the Tathāgata’s merit.
Seeking to emerge from entanglements and proceed toward liberation, I pray that the Buddha, out of his compassion, will graciously accept me;
may he kindle the lamp of wisdom within my dark chamber to shatter my doubts, ignorance, and the like.
Proclaiming the sublime Dharma-door of purity, Just as the Buddha traversed the path to Bodhi;
I bow my head to the peerless Great Physician King, Who fulfills my aspirations and eliminates all ailments.
May all delusive thoughts be utterly eradicated, And may I cast off the evil realms to reach the further shore.
Forever emerged from the great ocean of afflictions, Constantly practicing the Tathāgata’s Eightfold Noble Path.
Thus, speak the truth for my sake; I shall practice exactly as the Buddha has taught.
Resolutely seeking unexcelled, great Bodhi, I shall cultivate the true conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Accomplishing the inexhaustible retribution of merit, Relinquishing worldly life for the life of the Dharma,
Forever severing all fetters and bonds, One ultimately perfects the path to Bodhi.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Rakṣita:
"At that time, the Tathāgata Arthasiddhi, seeing that the prince’s faith was pure and his roots of goodness fully ripened, immediately proclaimed for him the Dharma of the bodhisattva practices."

Having heard this Dharma, Prince Puṇyaprabha attained the gate of dhāraṇī, realized wondrous liberation, and accomplished the five supernormal powers; he leaped into the air and scattered flowers as an offering.
Having made these offerings, they descended from the midst of the sky and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised the Tathāgata, speaking in verse:
"Homage to our Buddha of true golden hue, Whose marks and signs are most sublime and whose face is like the moon;
Whose merit and wisdom are peerless, Forever transcending the three realms of existence and eternally pure."
The Sage’s conch-like topknot is deep azure-blue, Lofty, prominent, and pure as Mount Sumeru.

I behold the peerless and boundless Buddha; The light from the hair-tuft between his brows shines everywhere, Like a *kumuda* flower or the bright moon, Surpassing white jade, snow, and mother-of-pearl.
Such a pure and great radiance dispels the darkness of the sins of sentient beings.
Your eyes are clear and brilliant like blue lotuses; you always regard us with a compassionate countenance.
Viewing enemies and kin without distinction in equanimity, both the sentient and the insentient receive benefit.
The tongue is like red copper, broad and long; it may cover the face or the great trichiliocosm.
Adapting to the capacities of beings, it flows forth as the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, universally rescuing all who suffer in the world.
I now prostrate to the Tathāgata’s teeth, Forty in number, even and closely set, white as jade;
The four canine fangs are as sharp as adamant, All emitting radiance to deliver all beings.
I now pay homage to the Buddha’s words of truth, Free from all falsehood and ornate rhetoric;
He has mastered the profound texts on nature and characteristics, Dispelling darkness and removing delusion across hundreds of thousands of lands.
The Brahma King, Śakra, the World-Protectors, the eight classes of nāgas and devas, and those in the three miserable realms—
all who were touched by this light had their suffering and affliction removed, and together they emerged from the ocean of saṃsāric birth and death.
Our Buddha’s calves are like those of the deer king; his gait is like that of the bull king, steady in its lifting.
When he sets foot upon the ground, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth all tremble.
Our Buddha’s physical marks are wondrously dignified; his skin is soft and of a true golden hue.
Peerless throughout all the worlds, sentient beings never tire of beholding you.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of past kalpas, the Buddha was able to relinquish everything to benefit sentient beings, causing them all to leave suffering behind and escape the cage of affliction; I now pay homage to the Great Compassionate Father.

The Buddha bestows the wealth of the Dharma upon all; his morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are all perfectly clear and bright. I now pay homage to the Buddha’s peerless wisdom;
my Buddha is the fearless Great Lion, able to shatter the boundless demons of affliction.
Skillfully healing all ailments, you eliminate them entirely; I now prostrate to you who have extinguished the three poisons.
Your actions of body, speech, and mind are free from defilement; unattached to the triple world, you are like a lotus risen from the water.
Your Brahma-voice is profound and wondrous like that of the Brahma-heaven; the voices of the kalaviṅka and the peacock cannot compare to yours.
I now pay homage to the Buddha, who has emerged from the three realms of existence;
he constantly contemplates the world as an illusion, a dream, or a flash of lightning that does not endure for long, devoid of person, devoid of self, and devoid of sentient beings.
The Dharma is fundamentally empty and quiescent, without arising; unable to know or awaken to this, beings wander through the cycle of rebirth.
Out of compassion, you extensively act for the sake of all sentient beings, skillfully proclaiming the wondrous Dharma according to their capacities.
The Great Sage, King of Physicians, to whom all turn in refuge, Constantly treats old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and affliction;
Thus he universally benefits all sentient beings, Causing each to follow the path of the Sugata for humans and devas.
Thus the Lord of Sages, with his compassion, Constantly pities those wandering through the six realms of saṃsāra, Like ants circling in an endless loop;
He leads these deluded and blind ones onto the true path.
Thus, by realizing awakening according to the Dharma, one possesses mastery over the Dharma to benefit the world;
as for the Eightfold Noble Path taught by the Buddha, those who hear it find delight and give rise to reverence.
The Buddha’s voice is subtle and wondrous, surpassing that of Brahmā, the Gandharvas, the Kinnaras, and the exquisite tones of all the goddesses;
it is unlike theirs, for the Buddha’s voice abounds in skillful means.
The merit of their pure and resonant speech is universal; sentient beings hear it according to their respective kinds.
Thus they ride upon the vehicle toward Bodhi, each one transcending the mundane and attaining liberation.
By making offerings of various supreme and wondrous things to the Buddha, one obtains the highest merit of humans and devas;
one may become a sovereign emperor or a high minister, constantly enjoying great wealth and immense happiness;
or one may become a Golden-Wheel King of the four continents, fully endowed with a thousand sons and the seven treasures.
Constantly practicing the ten wholesome deeds to benefit the world, all sentient beings follow and accord with them;
whether as a protector of the world (Lokapāla), or in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, or dwelling in Yāma, Tuṣita,
up to Paranirmita-vaśavartin and the Brahma heavens— all these are attained through making offerings to the Buddhas.
Thus, by seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, one is able to transcend all suffering and affliction;
it prevents one from falling into the evil realms, leading instead to peace, tranquility, and freedom from defilement.
The Buddha is able to dwell securely within all worlds, causing those who seek merit to attain it;
thus the merit they obtain continues long and uninterrupted, remaining inexhaustible for many millions of eons.
This most supreme and subtle adorned realm is free from defilement for those beings born therein;
their bodies radiate light surpassing that of gods and humans, and their actions of body, speech, and mind are all utterly pure.
Accomplishing various marks of merit, With fame spreading throughout all worlds,
Respected and loved by both gods and humans— Such a person attains these through making offerings to the Buddhas.
Our Buddha has long been free from all suffering and affliction; The buddha-fields of the ten directions all praise him, And the entire assembly takes refuge in him;
There is none who does not love and delight in his compassionate countenance.
I now prostrate before the Honored One among Men, Whose mark is unconditioned, serene and unmoving;
May I attain the realization of the five supernormal powers, And stand poised in the void to extol the Buddha.
I prostrate to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who is fearless, stainless, pure, and transcendent;
may all the virtues for which he is praised be dedicated so that humans and devas may attain perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla:

"At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the Devaputra Prabhāsa suddenly heard a great sound of wailing within the palace city of Prince Puṇyaprabha. He was struck with alarm and filled with anxiety and fear, not knowing whether it portended good or ill fortune."
Immediately, he brought his ministers and their retinues to the prince’s palace and asked the women of the court:
"Why were you weeping during the night?"
Then the palace attendants immediately reported to the king, saying:
"Prince Puṇyaprabha has suddenly departed from the palace; we know not where he has gone. We are filled with anxiety, fear, and deep sorrow, and for this reason we weep."

At that time, having heard these words, the Devaputra Prabhāsa felt as if his feet had stepped upon a precipice; he suddenly collapsed to the ground and remained unconscious for a long while before reviving.
Rising from the earth, his heart was filled with grief and distress; weeping and wailing, he desired to travel to every one of the thousand cities to search for him everywhere.
At that time, the holy sage who protected the city of Priyaṃkara addressed the king, saying:
"Prince Puṇyaprabha has gone to the east to pay homage, visit, and make offerings to the Buddha Saṃmatyartha."

When the Devaputra Prabhāsa heard these words, he immediately took eighty-four koṭis of palace ladies and maidservants, along with hundreds of thousands of nayutas of attendants and retinues surrounding him on all sides, and proceeded toward the east to the place where the Tathāgata Arthasiddhārtha resided.

Having arrived, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground at the feet of the World-Honored One. Standing to one side, he joined his palms toward the Buddha and praised him in verse:
"I bow my head in refuge to the Ocean of Merit, The peerless Honored One of wondrous, profound, and total retention;
To whom the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, turn for refuge— All gaze upon the Buddha without ever being satiated."
With the thirty-two marks, wondrously sublime and majestic, Adorned with the seven treasures, rare in this world;
Lofty, brilliant, and magnificent like a mountain of exquisite gold— You who transcend the world, I take refuge and pay homage.
Throughout inconceivable *koṭi* aeons in the past, you practiced and made offerings to *koṭi*s of Buddhas;
having deeply planted roots of virtue so vast and boundless, you have accomplished the Buddha-body with its wondrous marks and signs.
Through the practices of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, And through diligence, meditative concentration, and skillful means,
Having thus perfected these sublime deeds through successive cultivation, The physical marks are perfectly radiant and shine with brilliant light.
The light of the sun, the moon, lightning, and mani-jewels;
the bodily radiance of Śakra and Brahmā—when these lights are confronted by the Buddha’s light, they all vanish at once and are no longer seen.
The Buddha’s body appears like the moon reflected in water; his manifestations likewise accord with the capacities of beings.
He entered his mother’s womb riding upon an elephant in a dream, relinquishing his sovereign rank as the Lord of Tuṣita Heaven.
The Buddha’s body is signless like empty space; appearing born into the human world, he saves all beings.
At his first birth, he took seven steps as Śakra followed him; among gods and men, he is the most supreme.

That Buddha has no dharma he does not fully know; Without a teacher, he mastered the scriptures through his own understanding, And having attained the samādhi of tranquility, He rescues all beings from suffering and brings them to liberation.
Having renounced his parents and kinsmen, he departed from that royal city to enter the deep mountains;
surrounded by tens of millions of celestial hosts, he subdued the four Māras and attained perfect enlightenment.
Observing that this world is not ultimate, and seeing sentient beings submerged and wandering in saṃsāra,
you extend compassion and turn the wheel of Dharma for them, so that they may leave behind impermanence and emerge from suffering.
The Buddha has realized the dharma of tranquil extinction and purity;
Having perfected merit, wisdom, and skillful means, the Muni manifests emanations and bodily radiance; Thus, he is fully endowed with all such marks of a Buddha.
I pay homage to the Muni of boundless wisdom; I pay homage to the one who has fully realized the dharmas of the entire dharma-realm.
Though you know that all things are like illusions, without coming or going, you extend compassion to universally rescue all sentient beings.
Excellent!
The Buddha has taught the path to enlightenment, leading those sentient beings to attain bodhi. Such is the true Dharma that I seek; the true Dharma can deliver the world from suffering.
Our Buddha constantly dwells within the three realms of existence, Healing the maladies of all afflictions;
By means of my praise of the Buddha’s merits, I dedicate this toward enlightenment and all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:

"The Tathāgata Arthasiddhi, seeing this Devaputra Prabhāsa taking refuge, offering praise, and seeking liberation with firm faith, preached the Dharma for him in accordance with the king's intention."
At that time, upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, the Devaputra Prabhāsa immediately attained non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Then, Prince Puṇyaprabha, seeing his father the King take refuge in that Buddha, conceived a heart of faith and reverence; he immediately approached the Buddha, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!"
"I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will go to the city of Priyāṅgu and accept my offering of food and drink.
At that time, the Tathāgata Siddhārthamati silently granted his consent, accepting the Prince's invitation.
At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha addressed his father the king and all his kinsmen, saying:
"I now invite the Buddha; I shall offer my palace, gardens, groves, and all manner of precious ornaments as a gift to the Buddha for his worship."
"O you kinsmen and retinue, do not create obstacles or harbor stinginess; with one voice and in harmony, give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy.
At that time, the father-king and all his kinsmen spoke in unison, saying:
"We pray that he may relinquish all he possesses to offer as a gift to the Buddha; we shall all rejoice in this."
“At that time, the Tathāgata Arthasiddhi, surrounded by a respectful retinue of bhikṣus, entered the city of Priyāṅkara to receive their offerings.
Then, Prince Puṇyaprabha provided five hundred thousand carts of exquisite food and drink as an offering to the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.”

Furthermore, Prince Puṇyaprabha constructed a saṃghārāma for the Buddha and the assembly out of the seven precious gems on a vast scale, adorning its four sides with countless nets and parasols made of maṇi jewels.
Furthermore, he provided hundreds of thousands of couches and bedding, spread with exquisite garments upon them.
Moreover, on both sides of the vihāra, he arranged flowers, fruits, trees, flowing springs, and bathing pools; within those pools grew *puṇḍarīka* and *utpala* lotuses and other such blossoms.
Furthermore, before each and every bhikṣu, he prostrated with his head at their feet and offered a saṃghāṭī robe; he did likewise three times every day.

For thirty koṭis of years, he practiced austerities day and night, neither sleeping nor reclining, and without weariness. He neither bathed nor washed himself, nor did he adorn himself with perfumes or garlands. Free from anger and craving, he did not even begrudge his own body or life for the sake of the Dharma, let alone external wealth.
"Acting according to what the Buddha has taught and practicing as he has instructed, [the King] even brought about the meaning and intent until the Tathāgata Arthasiddhi entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Prince performed the cremation of the Tathāgata with red sandalwood."

All the various exquisite and renowned flowers, flower garlands, unguents, powdered incenses, and diverse musical instruments within Jambudvīpa were used to make offerings to the relics at the site of the cremation.
At that time, all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa came together to make offerings with incense, flowers, food, and drink, continuing in this manner for hundreds of thousands of years.

"At that time, Prince Puṇyaprabha collected the Buddha’s relics and constructed ninety-four koṭis of stūpas made of the seven precious gems, all of which were adorned on every side with nets of pearls."
Furthermore, before each stupa were erected five hundred parasols made of the seven precious gems, as well as flowers, fruits, trees, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments.
Moreover, before each and every stupa were placed hundreds of thousands of oil-lamp basins, with hundreds of thousands of lamps burning within each single basin.

Thus he made offerings for one *koṭi* of years; thereafter, the prince left the household life, shaved his head, and assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu. He practiced the dhūta austerities, went on alms rounds with his bowl, and subdued and severed the afflictions. For four *koṭis* of years, he constantly practiced the gift of Dharma, never wearying, just as the Buddha had done.

"At that time, the city guardians and holy ones of the city of Priyaṃkara, all the minor kings, the palace ladies, their retinues, and all sentient beings followed the Prince’s example by leaving the household life, shaving their hair, and practicing pure conduct."
At that time, the Śuddhaprabha devaputras said to one another:
"Since all the minor kings and the common people have all gone forth into homelessness, we shall go there to serve the Prince, just as one makes offerings to the Triple Gem."
"At that time, the monk Puṇyaprabha fully received, upheld, and mastered without obstruction all sixty-four koṭis of Dharma treasuries spoken by the Tathāgata Arthasiddhi."

In this way, the bhikṣu Puṇyaprabha had already drawn near to ninety-four koṭis of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas; at the abodes of each of those Buddhas, he made offerings without fail, and they were all just like those made to the Tathāgata Arthasiddhi, without any difference.
"At that time, was the Devaputra Prabhāsa anyone else?
He is none other than the present Tathāgata Amitāyus.
At that time, was Prince Puṇyaprabha anyone else?"
I myself am that person.
At that time, was the noble protector of the city in the city of Priyāṅgudhvaja anyone else?
It was none other than the present Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:

"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should study the example of that bhikṣu Puṇyaprabha by distancing themselves from craving, associating with virtuous friends, practicing the conduct of tranquility, and diligently making offerings to the Buddhas; before long, they shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha said, “Rāṣṭrapāla!

If there is another person who is greedily attached to gain and offerings, food and drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, respect, and praise, that person is deluded; they will become arrogant, violate the precepts, be false and insincere, slander the śramaṇas, and distance themselves from the Buddha-dharma. They will be inconsistent in body, speech, and mind, possessing only outward appearances while their minds lack tranquility. Being without shame or remorse, they remain far removed from the Buddha-field and far removed from Bodhi.”
Therefore, Rāṣṭrapāla!
Having heard this Dharma, you should understand it thus, you should study it thus, and you should practice it thus; you must not associate with evil friends or with gain and profit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If a person craves gain and offerings, They distance themselves from true and pure practice;
Because of this, they fall away from the Buddha’s Bodhi, Sinking forever into the path of birth and death for kalpas.”
Lacking shame and lacking remorse, never knowing contentment, Constantly driven by craving and greed, forever bound,
They do not fear the suffering and afflictions of the three miserable realms, Yet still they say:
"I am endowed with all virtuous conduct."
Falsely manifesting a state of tranquility while dwelling among the mountains, their minds are constantly bound by fame and profit;
people avoid them as they would a venomous snake, remaining long in saṃsāra without liberation.
If a person does not delight in the Dharma of the Tathāgata and treats with contempt the virtuous Saṃgha of bhikṣus,
they will forever depart from the celestial realms and fall into the evil paths; even if born into the human world, they will fall into the eight difficulties,
where for billions of kalpas it will be difficult to encounter a Buddha or hear the True Dharma he has taught.
If one encounters this for even a moment and acts accordingly, that person will surely realize the fruit of Bodhi.
The sublime practice and virtue of the Buddha-vehicle are inconceivable; all Tathāgatas emerge from it.
If a person feels aversion toward it yet delights in worldly toil, they will forever lose the unsurpassed path of Bodhi.
If a person possesses wisdom and skillful means, remains far removed from all faults and transgressions,
and compassionately rescues the sentient beings of the five destinies, that person’s conduct is identical to the conduct of the Buddha.
Though dwelling in the deep mountains and secluded places, they falsely manifest a sense of purity and loftiness for their own sake;
concealing the conduct of others, they speak of their own abilities, saying:
"I constantly recite ten million buddha-names every day."
If one gives rise to reverence for the Dharma of practice, seeking it with single-minded devotion without begrudging even body or life,
and acts according to the true teachings as I have spoken— such a person is not far from realizing Bodhi.
The Great Sage’s True Dharma is the supreme vehicle; It forever eliminates all burning afflictions.
If one practices with diligence according to what has been heard, One will ultimately and swiftly realize the unsurpassed path.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Rakṣita, saying:

"If various bodhisattvas were to practice the five pāramitās for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), it would not equal a person who, for a brief moment, hears, believes, understands, and upholds this True Dharma. Such merit surpasses the former merit such that the former does not approach even one hundredth part, one thousandth part, one hundred-thousand-koṭi part, nor even a calculable fraction; it does not even approach a metaphorical fraction."
When the Buddha preached this sutra, thirty nayutas of devas and humans in the assembly resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained the stage of non-retrogression;
seven thousand bhikṣus exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda-kṣānti*).
At that time, the Venerable Rakṣita addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This sutra is truly rare.
How should it be received and upheld?"
"What should it be named?
The Buddha said,
"Rāṣṭrapāla!"
This sutra is titled "The True Dharma of the Mahāyāna," and it is also titled "The Joyful Bodhisattva Practice of the Householder Puṇyakaraśmipratijñāviśuddhāpramāṇa"; thus should it be upheld.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Rakṣita, along with the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Questions of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Four: The Radiant Sparrow.
